title: The Song of the Vineyard and Six Woes
summary: Isaiah sings a love song about a friend's vineyard that received every care but produced only sour grapes, then reveals that the vineyard is Israel and Judah: God looked for justice and found bloodshed. Six woes follow, against land-grabbing, drunkenness, cynical mockery of God, calling evil good, self-conceit, and bribery. The chapter ends with God raising a banner for a distant nation whose army comes swiftly and roars like lions.
story: Chapters 2 to 4 closed with a hopeful picture of a cleansed Zion. Chapter 5 returns to the present and explains, through a parable, why judgment is necessary. God had done everything for his people: rescued them, planted them in the land, and given them his law. Their response was injustice. The six woes (woe is a cry of mourning, as at a funeral) spell out what the sour grapes look like in daily life. The chapter's last section, with its refrain that God's anger is not turned away and his hand is still upraised, links to a series of poems in 9:8 to 10:4 that use the same refrain, and it introduces the foreign army, later identified as Assyria, that God will use as his instrument.
historical:
The social sins condemned here fit Judah in the eighth century BC, a time of prosperity under Uzziah and Jotham when wealth concentrated in fewer hands. Isaiah's contemporary Micah makes the same charge against those who covet fields and seize them (Micah 2:1-2), and Amos had said similar things in the north. Israel's law intended land to stay with families as an inheritance from God (Leviticus 25:23), and the Jubilee law returned land to its original families every fifty years, though there is little evidence it was regularly practiced.

Verses 26 to 30 describe a disciplined, tireless army summoned from far away. Isaiah does not name it here, but chapter 7 and chapter 10 identify God's instrument as Assyria, whose armies under Tiglath-pileser III (reigned 745 to 727 BC) and his successors were the most effective military force of the age. Assyrian palace reliefs show exactly what Isaiah describes: archers with drawn bows, chariots, and cavalry. Verse 13 speaks of exile, which the northern kingdom suffered after 722 BC and Judah after 587 or 586 BC.
cultural:
Vineyards were a major investment in Israel's hill country. A farmer had to clear the rocky soil, terrace the slope, plant choice vines, build a stone watchtower where he could guard the crop at harvest, and cut a winepress into the bedrock. It took years before the vines produced. A vineyard that yielded sour, wild grapes after all that labor was a disaster. The song begins as though it were a love song (Isaiah sings for his beloved, and vineyards were a common image in love poetry, as in the Song of Songs), which drew listeners in before the turn.

The measures in verse 10 show the scale of the curse. Ten acres (literally ten yokes, the land ten teams of oxen could plow in a day) would produce only a bath of wine, about six gallons or twenty-two liters. A homer of seed (roughly a donkey's load) would yield an ephah of grain, a tenth of a homer. The harvest would return less than was sown. Sheol in verse 14 is the realm of the dead, pictured as a hungry mouth. Feasts with lyres, harps, tambourines, and flutes (verse 12) were the entertainment of the rich; the prophets objected not to music or wine but to luxury that ignored God and the poor.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 7 are a parable in the form of a song, which draws the hearers into judging the case (verse 3) before revealing that they are the accused, much as Nathan did with David (2 Samuel 12). The climax in verse 7 rests on two Hebrew wordplays that English cannot reproduce: God looked for mishpat (justice) and saw mispach (bloodshed), for tsedaqah (righteousness) and heard tse'aqah (a cry of distress). The words sound almost the same but mean opposites. Verses 8 to 25 contain six woes, interrupted by therefore sections that announce consequences. Verses 26 to 30 describe the coming army with mounting speed and noise, and end in darkness.

outline.t: Woe to those who join house to house
Woe to the drunkards who ignore God's work
Woe to those who mock God's plan
Woe to those who call evil good
Woe to the wise in their own eyes
Woe to the corrupt judges, and God's anger

doctrines.note: The vineyard song shows that judgment is not arbitrary. God asks what more he could have done, and the answer is nothing. Judgment comes because a people given every grace produced injustice.

The woes show sin in social and economic forms: greed for land, self-indulgence, cynicism, moral confusion, arrogance, and corruption. Verse 20's calling evil good is the end point, where conscience itself is inverted.
Verse 16 states a key principle: the holy God shows himself holy in righteousness. His holiness is not only separateness but moral perfection displayed in just judgment.
God whistles for a distant nation, and it comes. The empires of the world are instruments in his hand, a theme Isaiah develops fully in chapter 10.

words.note: Kerem, vineyard, used seven times in this chapter. The vineyard became a standard image for Israel (Psalm 80:8-16; Jeremiah 2:21), and Jesus built his parable of the tenants on this passage. The image carries both God's care and his expectation of fruit.

Mispach, bloodshed or outpouring, found only here in the Hebrew Bible. Isaiah seems to have chosen it for its sound: it is one letter away from mishpat, justice. God looked for justice and found its grotesque counterfeit.
Hoy, woe or alas, a cry used in mourning for the dead (1 Kings 13:30). When prophets pronounce woe on the living, they are announcing a funeral in advance. The word appears six times in this chapter.

christ: Jesus retold this parable in his own ministry. In the parable of the tenants (Mark 12:1-12; Matthew 21:33-46; Luke 20:9-19) he describes a man who planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress, and built a tower, using the details of Isaiah 5:2, and then sent servants and finally his own son to collect the fruit. The religious leaders understood he was speaking of them. In John 15 Jesus calls himself the true vine and his followers the branches, promising that those who remain in him will bear fruit. Where Israel as God's vineyard failed to produce justice, Jesus is the faithful vine, and through union with him God's people bear the fruit God always sought.

hard.q: Is God harsh to destroy the vineyard he planted?
hard.a: The song anticipates this objection by putting the hearers in the judge's seat (verse 3) and asking what more the owner could have done (verse 4). The point is that the judgment is fitting: the owner removes the protection he had provided, and the vineyard returns to wilderness. Several things soften a reader's first impression. The judgment is described mostly as God withdrawing care rather than actively attacking (verses 5-6). The fruit God wanted was not religious performance but justice and righteousness, especially for the vulnerable. And the rest of the book shows that this is not the end of the vineyard: in 27:2-6 Isaiah sings a second vineyard song in which God guards and waters his vineyard and Israel fills the world with fruit. Judgment here serves a purpose beyond itself.

questions: Verse 20 describes people who call evil good and good evil. How do individuals and cultures come to invert right and wrong, and how can we notice it in ourselves?
God looked for justice and found bloodshed. What fruit do you think God is looking for in your life and community?
Jesus retold this parable about the leaders of his day. What would it look like for religious people today to hear it as addressed to them?
